# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

The **2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado** was an **EF-3 tornado** that struck the U.S. state of Alabama on April 27, 2011, as part of the **2011 Super Outbreak**, one of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in American history . The tornado traveled a path of approximately **72 miles** through Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties in central Alabama, with peak winds of **145 mph** . It resulted in **7 fatalities and 50 injuries**, with most casualties occurring in Hale County near the Talladega National Forest .

## Meteorological synopsis

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was one of **330 confirmed tornadoes** that formed during the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak, including **292 tornadoes in 16 states on April 27 alone** . The tornado touched down at approximately **5:30 p.m.** CDT in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive . It tracked northeastward through rural Greene County north of Forkland before crossing the Black Warrior River into Hale County west of Sawyerville .

The tornado intensified as it crossed Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, reaching its peak intensity of **EF-3 with winds of 145 mph** . It continued northeastward, crossing several county roads and Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill before entering the Talladega National Forest near Ingram . The tornado maintained EF-3 intensity as it moved through Eoline, causing significant structural damage, before weakening to EF-2 with winds of 125 mph as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton . It eventually lifted just northeast of Marvel .

## Damage and impact

The tornado caused extensive damage across its path, destroying or damaging numerous structures in all three counties it affected . In Greene County, the tornado damaged or destroyed at least **4 mobile homes, 3 outbuildings, and 2 churches**, along with numerous trees, resulting in **2 minor injuries** .

The most severe damage and casualties occurred in Hale County. As the tornado crossed into Hale County and intensified to EF-3 strength, it caused **at least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities** . The tornado destroyed or damaged numerous mobile homes and single-family homes, along with one church, and knocked down thousands of trees . The tornado then entered the Talladega National Forest, where it caused significant tree damage before emerging into Bibb County .

In Bibb County, the tornado moved through Eoline, where it caused significant structural damage consistent with EF-3 intensity . The tornado destroyed **a dozen mobile homes and single-family homes**, along with the **Eoline Fire Department and another business** . One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire department, and at least **10 other injuries** were reported .

The tornado's path was approximately **72.13 miles long** with a maximum width of **1,760 yards (1 mile)** . The tornado was classified as an EF-3 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale with peak winds of 145 mph .

## Notable characteristics

One of the most remarkable aspects of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was its **unusually high kinetic energy** for an EF-3 tornado. According to scientific analysis, it had an estimated total kinetic energy of **123 terajoules (TJ)**, making it the most energetic tornado examined in a 2014 study of recent U.S. tornadoes . This is particularly significant because, while the average total kinetic energy for EF-3 tornadoes in the study was 40.1 TJ, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado had more than three times that amount .

The tornado's damage path was also notable for its **diverse damage ratings**. Analysis of the damage path showed that 30% of the path had EF-0 damage, 25% had EF-1 damage, 38% had EF-2 damage, and 7% had EF-3 damage . This distribution is unusual for an EF-3 tornado, which typically has a higher percentage of its path at the highest damage rating.

## Emergency response and recovery

The April 27, 2011 tornado outbreak was so extensive and devastating that federal emergency management officials became engaged with Alabama communities from day one . The **Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)** deployed long-term community recovery staff to work with state and local governments throughout the recovery process .

Within days of the storms, key project and planning professionals were embedded with local governments to assess damage and provide assistance . These professionals helped answer city officials' primary questions: "Where do we go from here and how do we get there?" .

The state of Alabama received nearly **\$74 million** from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in two separate allocations to assist with recovery efforts . Governor Robert Bentley established the **Governor's Emergency Relief Fund (GERF)** in May 2011 to help with unmet recovery needs .

The recovery process involved extensive community engagement. FEMA's long-term recovery specialists met with leaders of the 15 most severely damaged communities to provide information about partnering with FEMA and the **Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA)** . Support was also enlisted from nonprofits, religious organizations, chambers of commerce, and other local resources .

## Legacy and significance

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is significant for several reasons. First, it was part of the **deadliest tornado outbreak in the United States since the 1925 Tri-State Tornado**, with at least 340 fatalities across the four-day outbreak . In Alabama alone, 249 deaths were confirmed by the morning of April 30 .

Second, the tornado's exceptional kinetic energy has made it a subject of scientific study. Its 123 TJ of energy is more than twice the average for EF-4 tornadoes (36.5 TJ) and nearly 2.5 times the average for EF-5 tornadoes (50.4 TJ) in the study sample . This unusual energy profile has prompted researchers to examine factors that might contribute to such high energy in a tornado of this rating.

Third, the tornado highlighted the vulnerability of rural communities to severe weather. Many of the fatalities occurred in mobile homes, which are particularly susceptible to tornado damage . The destruction of the Eoline Fire Department also demonstrated how critical infrastructure can be compromised during such events .

The recovery from the 2011 tornadoes, including the Sawyerville–Eoline event, led to improved building codes and emergency management practices in Alabama. Communities worked with FEMA and other agencies to develop long-term recovery plans that emphasized sustainable building practices and community resilience .

The tornado's path through three counties also demonstrated the challenges of coordinating emergency response across multiple jurisdictions. Tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from 4:50 p.m. until 7:45 p.m., providing residents with advance notice of the approaching danger .

## Conclusion

The 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado stands as a significant event in American meteorological history, combining exceptional power with tragic consequences. As one of the most energetic tornadoes ever recorded for its rating, it continues to fascinate researchers studying tornado dynamics and energy transfer . The tornado's impact on rural Alabama communities underscored both the destructive power of severe weather and the resilience of affected populations in rebuilding their lives and communities.

The event also contributed to advances in emergency management and recovery planning, with lessons learned informing future responses to natural disasters . The \$74 million in federal recovery funding and the establishment of long-term community recovery programs demonstrated the commitment of federal and state governments to helping affected communities rebuild stronger than before .

Today, the communities affected by the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado have largely recovered, though reminders of the event remain. The destruction of the Eoline Fire Department and the loss of seven lives serve as sobering reminders of the power of nature and the importance of preparedness . Yet the stories of heroism, community support, and successful recovery that emerged from this tragedy also demonstrate the strength and determination of the human spirit in the face of adversity.

The scientific data collected from this tornado, particularly its unusual kinetic energy profile, continues to contribute to our understanding of tornado formation and behavior . As climate change and population growth increase the potential for future tornado disasters, the lessons learned from the 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado remain relevant for researchers, emergency managers, and communities across tornado-prone regions of the United States.

### 2011 Tornadoes

The State of Alabama received nearly $74 million dollar from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in two separate allocations to assist in the recovery efforts of the areas impacted by the tornadoes of April 2011.

The State qualified 36 counties in northern half of the State and awarded projects based on competition.

The State awardees are – Birmingham ($625,000), Blount County ($758,572), Cordova ($5,098,515), Cullman City ($5,989,728.29), Cullman County ($1,294,892), DeKalb County ($1,573,172.29), Franklin County ($1,361,624), Hackleburg ($8,338,437.67), Haleyville ($523,876), Hanceville ($80,000), Marion County ($2,642,775.95), Moulton ($968,480), Phil Campbell ($3,212,201.16), Tuscaloosa ($8,470,000), Tuscaloosa County ($9,238,230), and Winston County ($912,200.07).

In addition, the State budgeted over $18 Million for repair and replacement of homes damaged by the storm in the most impacted and distressed counties.

To date, most funds have been expended, and all except for two projects have been closed.

2.title: Oleada de tornados en Estados Unidos del 25-28 de abril de 2011
2.content:
Una [oleada de tornados](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleada_de_tornados "Oleada de tornados") comenzó el 25 de abril de 2011, afectando al [Sur](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sur_de_Estados_Unidos "Sur de Estados Unidos") y Este de Estados Unidos con destrucción catastrófica, especialmente a través de [Alabama](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"). La oleada produjo destructivos tornados en [Alabama](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), [Arkansas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Georgia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(Estados_Unidos) "Georgia (Estados Unidos)"), [Misisipi](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misisipi "Misisipi"), [Carolina del Norte](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_del_Norte "Carolina del Norte"), [Tennessee](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") y [Virginia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") y afectó severamente otras áreas en todo el [Sur](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sur_de_Estados_Unidos "Sur de Estados Unidos") y Este de los Estados Unidos, con tornados confirmados desde [Texas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") a [Nueva York](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nueva_York_(estado) "Nueva York (estado)"). Generalizados y destructivos tornados ocurrieron en cada día de la oleada hasta ahora, aunque probablemente no tan grandes o numerosos, el 28 de abril.

Hasta el 6 de mayo de 2011, por lo menos 340 personas murieron como resultado del tornado, todas a excepción de cinco de las muertes ocurridas el 27 de abril. 249 de las muertes solo en el [estado de Alabama](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama") habían sido confirmadas por la [administración de desastres](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administraci%C3%B3n_de_desastres "Administración de desastres") hasta la mañana del 30 de abril. El 27 de abril fue el día más mortífero de tornados en los Estados Unidos desde el [tornado tri-estatal de 1925](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_tri-estatal_de_1925 "Tornado tri-estatal de 1925"), y el segundo día más mortífero de tornados desde 1950. 330 tornados confirmados se han formado en cuatro días, incluyendo 292 en 16 estados el 27 de abril. **_Sawyerville-Eoline (Greene,Hale and Bibb Counties)EF-3 Tornado April 27, 2011_** **Rating: [(_Click for EF Scale_)](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/enhancedfujitascale)****EF-3** **Estimated Maximum Wind:****145 mph** **Injuries/Fatalities:******50 Injuries /7 Fatalities**** **Damage Path Length:****72.13 miles** **Maximum Path Width:****1760 yards (1 mile)** **Approximate Start Point/Time:********32.6152/-88.0543 at 530 pm****** **Approximate End Point/Time:**************33.1524/-86.9898 at 655 pm************ **National Weather Service meteorologists surveyed multiple tracks across Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties. It has been determined that the damage was consistent with a strong tornado. The tornado touched down in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just West of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, and headed northeast across rural Greene County north of Forkland. At least 4 mobile homes, 3 outbuildings, and 2 churches were damaged or destroyed along with numerous trees. Two minor injuries were noted in Greene County. The track started as an EF-1 but increased to an EF-2 rating while in Greene County.** **The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and into Hale County west of Sawyerville. The tornado crossed AL Route 14, just north of Sawyerville, where it intensifyed to an EF-3 rating with winds of 145 mph. As the tornado continued northeast, it crossed CR 18, CR 21, AL Hwy 69 south of Harper Hill, and CR 29 east of Ingram. Extensive structural damage was noted in the these locations, which resulted in at least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes and one church were damaged or destroyed. Thousands of trees were knocked down. The tornado moved into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, where it caused significant tree damage to the Bibb County line.** **The tornado tracked northeastward where it caused significant tree damage in the national forest. The tornado moved through Eoline and caused significant structural damage consistent with an EF-3 rating and winds of 145 mph. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes sustained minor to major damage. A dozen mobile homes and single family homes were destroyed. In addition, the Eoline Fire Dept and another business were destroyed. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire dept. At least 10 other injuries were noted. The tornado continued northeast and crossed AL Hwy 5, south of West Blocton where it weakened slightly to an EF-2 with winds of 125 mph. Several mobile homes and single family homes sustained major damage or were destroyed near CR 26. Along the path, thousands of trees were downed. The tornado continued to weaken and lifted just northeast of Marvel.** **Tornado Warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties from 450 pm until 745 pm.** [View larger map](https://noaa.maps.arcgis.com/apps/Embed/index.html?webmap=15f53603ceb9435aaa60c1d49a1c125c&extent=-87.7993,32.6514,-87.1264,33.1381&zoom=true&scale=true&legend=true&basemap_gallery=true&disable_scroll=true&theme=light) **Radar Data** [![Image 10: Radar Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/r2255.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/r2255.gif)[![Image 11: Radar Image](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/v2255.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/bmx/significant_events/2011/042711/sawyerville/v2255.gif) **This is an image of the 0.5 degree reflectivity data from KBMX at 555 pm as the circulation was over Sawyerville. HACKLEBURG – As Alabama continues to rebuild and recover after deadly tornadoes devastated more than half of Alabama’s counties on April 27, 2011, Governor Robert Bentley on Wednesday visited one of the hardest hit areas to assess the progress five years later and highlight the state’s response.

“Alabama will never forget the more than 250 people who lost their lives on April 27, 2011,” Governor Bentley said. “Today, five years later, Alabama is better prepared to face the next natural disaster due to the lessons learned in how we prepare and respond. I am proud of the efforts state agencies made to help communities recover.”

The Alabama Emergency Management Agency (AEMA) was the lead coordinating agency for 58 state and federal agencies during the response and recovery efforts for 35 counties and 80 cities impacted by the April 27, 2011 storms. The agency played a critical role in helping the state recover by providing help through Individual Assistance, Public Assistance, Hazard Mitigation grants and other programs. To date, Alabama has received over $361 million in grants and aid. Mitigation grants provided funding for nearly 4,500 residential safe rooms and community safe rooms.

“The coordination of state and federal agencies is critical in any response to a natural disaster, and Alabama is better prepared today than ever before,” AEMA Director Art Faulkner said. “Alabama’s unified response is a result of local, state and federal partnerships we have worked to establish during non-disaster times.”

In addition to AEMA, several other state agencies were instrumental in helping rebuild Alabama.

The Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA) provided cities and counties over $75 million in federal assistance grants. The Disaster Community Development Block Grant provided support for housing developments, infrastructure repair and debris removal.

Serve Alabama partnered with the United Ways of Alabama to help register volunteers to help in the recovery effort. They coordinated more than 52,000 volunteers in the field for a total of 325,095 volunteer hours. This does not include the tremendous effort of the affiliated volunteers serving through organizations like the Salvation Army, various religious organizations and the American Red Cross.

In May of 2011, Governor Bentley established the Governor’s Emergency Relief Fund (GERF) to help with unmet recovery needs that unfolded in the wake of the recent deadly tornado outbreak across the state. To date, more than $6 million has been raised for the GERF, and approximately $5.7 million has been spent to help fund community safe rooms which have been proven to save lives in a tornado and upgrade outdoor emergency warning systems to alert citizens to dangerous weather.

Governor Bentley also announced the creation of the [Alabama Disaster Recovery and Resiliency Task Force.](http://www.bentleygov.org/assets/2016/04/EO-19-Disaster-Recovery-Task-Force.pdf) The purpose of this task force is to make recommendations regarding comprehensive, strategic and long-term reforms that enhance the efficient and cost-effective delivery of emergency management services in Alabama. The Alabama Disaster Recovery and Resiliency Task Force will study the cost of disasters to Alabama and make recommendations regarding comprehensive, strategic and long-term reforms that enhance the efficient and cost effective delivery of emergency management services in Alabama.

“With the creation of the new Alabama Disaster Recovery and Resiliency Task Force, we will further the state’s effort to recover from future disasters by allowing this task force to review and recommend a stronger way to provide services need to help communities recover,” Governor Bentley added.
